description: Shared Data Integrity proof vectors for Trust Task documents. Every library's proof verifier runs every entry, so a document signed by one implementation is checked by all of them (SPEC §4.7). Signed with the Ed25519 key of seed [7; 32] unless noted. An entry's `exceptions` names a runtime that reaches a different result today, and why; that runtime's test asserts the exception, so it fails once the gap closes.

entries.why: The baseline suite every consumer verifies (SPEC §4.7.1). Its proofValue is reproduced byte for byte by the Rust, TypeScript, Dart and Go signers.
ecdsa-jcs-2019 over P-256, signed by the TypeScript backend. SPEC §4.7.1 says a consumer SHOULD verify P-256.
ecdsa-jcs-2019 over P-384, signed by the TypeScript backend.
ecdsa-jcs-2019 over P-256, signed by the Go backend with a high S, which every verifier must accept (Go's ecdsa.Sign does not normalise S). SPEC §4.7.1 says a consumer SHOULD verify P-256.
ecdsa-jcs-2019 over P-384, signed by the Go backend with a high S, which every verifier must accept (Go's ecdsa.Sign does not normalise S).

issuedAt is spelled 2026-01-01T00:00:00.000Z and expiresAt 2027-01-01T00:00:00+00:00, both valid RFC 3339 that a typed date parser re-serializes differently. A verifier that checks the document as received accepts it; one that re-serializes a typed parse refuses a correctly signed document (SPEC §4.7, What a consumer verifies).

The previous document with both timestamps rewritten to the Z form and the proof left as it was. It must fail: the signature covers the spelling, so a verifier that accepts this is not checking the bytes it received.

A process-attestation/0.1 attested response — the spec's own worked example, issued by the did:key Holder with proofPurpose authentication (the purpose SPEC §4.7.3 recommends and the registry's signers default to). Pins that a response carrying a receipt reference, a receipt digest and disclosed aggregates verifies in every library, so a Holder built on one library is checked by a Verifier built on another.

The same response with `disclosed.timeline.checkpointCount` altered after signing. The proof covers the disclosed aggregates, not only the envelope: a Holder cannot adjust what it disclosed without re-signing.
The baseline document correctly signed with proofPurpose keyAgreement. It must fail: a key-agreement key never authorises a signature (SPEC §4.7.3).

The baseline document correctly signed with proofPurpose `assertion`, which names no verification relationship. It must fail (SPEC §4.7.3): the purpose is the relationship the verifier checks, so one it does not recognise cannot be checked.
A correctly signed proof whose `expires` (2026-01-02T00:00:00Z) has passed. It must fail: VC Data Integrity §2.1 makes a proof unusable after its `expires`.

rust.why: Known gap: affinidi-data-integrity 0.8's proof type has no `expires` member and drops it when parsing, so the signature Rust recomputes leaves out a member the signer covered. trust-tasks-proof refuses any proof carrying `expires` as unsupported until the upstream type gains the member.

entries.why: A correctly signed proof whose `expires` (2999-01-01T00:00:00Z) has not passed. It verifies.

`expires` is 2999-02-30T00:00:00Z, a day February does not have. Every runtime checks each field of `expires` against its range after the shared pattern, rather than relying on its language's own date parser, which in one runtime or another rolls the value over or accepts it.

`expires` is 2999-01-01T24:00:00Z; hours run 00-23. Every runtime checks each field of `expires` against its range after the shared pattern, rather than relying on its language's own date parser, which in one runtime or another rolls the value over or accepts it.

`expires` is 2999-12-31T23:59:60Z; seconds run 00-59, and no runtime can know whether a leap second will be inserted. Every runtime checks each field of `expires` against its range after the shared pattern, rather than relying on its language's own date parser, which in one runtime or another rolls the value over or accepts it.

`expires` carries the offset +24:00; an offset is at most 14:00. Every runtime checks each field of `expires` against its range after the shared pattern, rather than relying on its language's own date parser, which in one runtime or another rolls the value over or accepts it.

`expires` carries the offset +23:60; offset minutes run 00-59. Every runtime checks each field of `expires` against its range after the shared pattern, rather than relying on its language's own date parser, which in one runtime or another rolls the value over or accepts it.

`expires` carries the offset +99:00; an offset is at most 14:00. Every runtime checks each field of `expires` against its range after the shared pattern, rather than relying on its language's own date parser, which in one runtime or another rolls the value over or accepts it.

`created` is 2026-02-30T10:34:46Z: a day February does not have. `Date.parse` rolls it over into March. Correctly signed. Every runtime applies the ranges it applies to `expires` to `created` too, and refuses it as malformed.

`created` is 2026-09-15T24:00:00Z: hour 24. `Date.parse` reads it as the next day. Correctly signed. Every runtime applies the ranges it applies to `expires` to `created` too, and refuses it as malformed.

`created` is 2026-13-45T25:61:61Z: month 13, day 45, hour 25, minute and second 61. `Date.parse` gives NaN, which compares false with the clock-skew horizon, and `DateTime.parse` rolls it over into 2027. Correctly signed. Every runtime applies the ranges it applies to `expires` to `created` too, and refuses it as malformed.
`created` is 2026-06-30T23:59:60Z: a leap second. chrono reads it as one. Correctly signed. Every runtime applies the ranges it applies to `expires` to `created` too, and refuses it as malformed.

`created` is 2026-09-16T10:34:46+24:00: an offset of 24 hours. Go's `time.Parse` accepts it. Correctly signed. Every runtime applies the ranges it applies to `expires` to `created` too, and refuses it as malformed.

Issued by the did:key of the Ed25519 identity point (a key of small order) with R the identity and S = 0. That signature satisfies [S]B = R + [k]A for every message, so a verifier that accepts small-order keys accepts any document from this issuer. RFC 8032 decoding as the libraries apply it, and verify_strict, refuse the key.
The same signature under the identity point encoded non-canonically (y = p + 1). RFC 8032 §5.1.3 refuses a y of p or more.

Signed by the seed-7 key with R = rB + T, T a point of order 8, and S = r + k·a. The cofactored equation holds and the cofactorless one does not. Every library checks the cofactorless equation (TypeScript checks it explicitly; @noble alone checks the cofactored one), so all four refuse it.
